## Added

- **Setting up is mostly done for you.** `r2b setup` can now sign you in
  to Cloudflare in your browser, and comes back knowing which account
  you are on and which R2 buckets you have — offering to make one if you
  have none. It used to ask for four things; it asks for two. It also
  links you straight to the exact page where your R2 token is made,
  instead of telling you to go and find it.

  The sign-in asks to manage R2 storage and to see which accounts you
  belong to. It does **not** ask for the two permissions that would let
  it read the files inside a bucket, and it is thrown away when setup
  finishes — nothing is kept, and your scheduled backups keep running on
  your own R2 keys as they always have.

  There is one thing it cannot do. Cloudflare deliberately offers no way
  for an application to create API tokens on your behalf, so the access
  key and secret still have to be made in the dashboard and pasted in.
  Everything around them is gone.

  If there is no browser to open — a server you reach over SSH — you are
  not asked, and setup works exactly as it did before.

- **A new Cost mode, showing what this is costing you.** How much is
  stored, how many operations you have used against Cloudflare's free
  allowance, and what the month is coming to, split between storage and
  operations. Press `3`, or run `r2b budget`.

  These are estimates, and the screen says so every time. Cloudflare
  publishes no bill that r2backup can read, so the figures are worked
  out from what r2backup itself did, at Cloudflare's published rates.
  Anything else on your account is not counted. Most people backing up a
  documents folder never leave the free tier, and it says that plainly
  rather than showing a row of zeroes.

- **A monthly spending limit, if you want one.** `r2b budget set 5`, or
  press `b` in the Cost mode. When the estimate reaches it, backups
  pause.

  Pause, not stop. `r2b budget continue`, or `c` in the Cost mode,
  carries on for the rest of the month — and the limit comes back on the
  1st by itself, so waving it through once does not quietly disable it
  forever. Reaching the limit is shown, not silent, because a backup
  that stops running otherwise looks exactly like a backup with nothing
  to do.

  **Restores are never paused**, whatever you have set and however much
  you have spent. Getting your data back is the reason the backups
  exist.

  There is no limit unless you set one, and r2backup will never set one
  for you.

- **Updates offer themselves.** When a command finishes, if there is a
  newer release, r2b says so and asks. Once a day at most, only when you
  are there to answer — a scheduled backup at 3am is never interrupted
  by it, and neither is anything piped or scripted. Set
  `R2BACKUP_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` to turn it off entirely.
